title: Silicon Valley Allies Push for Jensen Huang’s Reinstatement at Nvidia
author: Daniel Nenni
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Jensen Huang is considering a return as Nvidia’s chief executive, with Silicon Valley allies preparing a campaign to persuade the company’s board to reinstate him.

An unnamed supporter told the newspaper that allies were assembling a “war room” of technology executives to lobby directors and seek backing from the White House. The effort reportedly has Huang’s support, although no agreement on his return has been announced.

The potential comeback follows Huang’s resignation amid disclosures about extramarital relationships, including an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has been investigated by US authorities over suspected espionage. Reuters reported that Huang also had intimate relationships with two Nvidia employees, citing its own reporting and an earlier New York Times account.

The espionage allegations remain unproven. Beijing has denied that Alice Huang is a spy, and Reuters said it had not independently established whether she worked for the Chinese government. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related.

Nvidia’s regulatory filing states that its board accepted Huang’s resignation and appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive while searching for a permanent successor. Kress continues to hold her finance position.

The leadership turmoil has also prompted scrutiny of corporate oversight. Reuters reported that independent directors hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate the circumstances surrounding Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang.

Any reinstatement would leave directors weighing Huang’s influence against unresolved questions about trust, accountability and governance. His supporters’ lobbying campaign adds pressure while the company searches for leadership.

For now, the reported “war room” represents an effort to secure a comeback, rather than a confirmed return. Nvidia did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment on the report, and no reinstatement timetable has been publicly announced.

The article was based on these reports:

Reuters, November 15 — Huang’s possible comeback and allies’ “war room,” citing the Financial Times.
Financial Times — the original comeback report.
Reuters, November 13 — reporting on the relationships and investigation. It states that Reuters had not independently verified the espionage allegations.
